\paragraph{Residual DR Error Analysis.}
\label{app:residual-dr-analysis}

Across all fine-tuned settings (2 models $\times$ 2 datasets $\times$ full S1), only 36 domain/range violations remain.
Manual inspection reveals four root causes:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{Entity type errors} (39\%): the LLM assigns an incorrect entity type (e.g., labeling a geographic entity as \textsc{LOC} when the gold standard requires \textsc{MISC}), causing the semantic mask to permit a domain/range-incompatible relation.
\item \emph{Schema coverage gaps} (33\%): the frequency-based constraint table, constructed from training-set co-occurrence statistics, does not cover long-tail type pairs that are ontologically valid but rare. These violations are irreducible by decoding-time constraints alone.
\item \emph{Incorrect relation selection} (17\%): the model selects a semantically inappropriate relation whose domain/range constraints are incompatible with the correctly typed entities.
\item \emph{Direction reversal} (11\%): the model assigns the correct relation but inverts head/tail roles, placing entities in positions that violate the relation's asymmetric domain/range specification.
\end{enumerate}

Two dataset-specific patterns emerge.
Outside Llama DocRED, all residual violations (3 of 36, spanning Llama SciERC and Qwen DocRED) trace exclusively to schema coverage gaps---the model's entity typing is accurate, and the constraint system has reached its theoretical ceiling given the frequency-based constraint table.
On DocRED, Llama-3.1-8B contributes 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), with entity type errors as the dominant cause (14/33, 42\%).
This asymmetry reflects Llama's weaker fine-tuned entity typing on DocRED's larger ontology (96 relations, 7 entity types) compared to Qwen, which achieves near-zero residual.
The implication is twofold: (i)~the irreducible floor from schema gaps is small ($\sim$3 violations across 4 settings), confirming that the constraint system operates near its theoretical optimum; (ii)~residual violations from entity typing errors are addressable through stronger base models or improved entity typing modules, without modifying the constraint architecture.

The crossover point occurs when post-hoc rejection exceeds $\sim$70\%: Mistral DocRED rejects 73.7\% of predicted triples, discarding enough true positives that constrained decoding's recall advantage dominates ($+$1.67\,pp).
OntoCoDec's advantage thus scales with violation severity---precisely when constraints are most needed, post-hoc filtering is most destructive.
Under fine-tuning, both strategies converge because few violations remain to filter or constrain ($\Delta \leq 0.55$\,pp across all four FT groups, with each strategy winning two).

%%% FT Latency %%%

\paragraph{Fine-Tuned Latency Profiling.}
\label{app:ft-latency}
Under LoRA fine-tuning (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 100 documents, RTX PRO 6000), per-document inference times are: unconstrained 2.594\,s, grammar-only 2.637\,s ($+$1.7\%), semantic-only 2.625\,s ($+$1.2\%), full S1 2.655\,s ($+$2.3\%, $p{<}0.0001$ paired $t$-test).
The combined overhead is sub-additive (2.3\% $<$ 1.7\%$+$1.2\%) because fine-tuned models produce fewer grammar-first fallback events (the semantic mask conflicts with grammar-valid tokens less often when per-slot predictions are better calibrated), reducing the number of active masking calls per document.
Compared to the zero-shot regime (Table~\ref{tab:runtime}), absolute overhead decreases from seconds-scale to milliseconds-scale: the fine-tuned model generates shorter, more structured outputs, compressing total generation time from 8.69\,s to 2.594\,s per document.

%%% Fuzzy Relation Matching %%%

\paragraph{Relation Matching Protocol.}
\label{app:fuzzy-matching}
Relation F1 evaluation uses fuzzy normalization to handle model-specific formatting variants (e.g., underscores vs.\ spaces, abbreviations).
A predicted relation $r_p$ matches gold relation $r_g$ if: (1)~exact string match after case-insensitive normalization, or (2)~token overlap $>$80\% \emph{and} edit distance $\leq 2$.
This protocol affects primarily Mistral, which produces underscore-separated variants (e.g., ``head\_of\_government'' for ``head of government'').
On Mistral DocRED, fuzzy matching contributes 98 additional TPs ($+$0.84\,pp R-F1; strict R-F1\,=\,3.50\% vs.\ fuzzy 4.34\%).
For Qwen and Llama under grammar constraints, the grammar layer enforces exact relation names, making fuzzy matching irrelevant (0 additional matches).
All F1 figures in the main text use fuzzy normalization consistently across all models and conditions.

\label{app:beam-search}

OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.

(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Beam search ($k{=}4$) vs.\ greedy decoding under full S1 constraints.
SciERC evaluated on full test set (551 documents); DocRED evaluated on 50-document subsets (greedy baselines from 998-document full evaluation, not matched subsets).
ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:beam-search}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.53} & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / DocRED (50$^\dagger$)}
  & Greedy$^*$  & 0 & 0.03 & 10.21 & 2.57 & 59.37 & 8.23 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / DocRED (50$^\dagger$)}
  & Greedy$^*$  & 0 & 0 & 2.57 & 12.13 & 55.01 & 6.27 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.94} & 55.62 & 9.47 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 13.40 & 1.27 & 27.46 & 3.67 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / DocRED (50$^\dagger$)}
  & Greedy$^*$  & 0 & 0 & 33.21 & 0.19 & 50.59 & 5.52 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{21.37} & 0.19 & 51.78 & 5.70 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (10.21\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (2.57\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 79\% and 92\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.2\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 35\% relative (33.2\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters grammar$\cap$semantic$=$\emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-ablation} varies beam width $k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ on Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551 documents) under full S1 constraints.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect of beam width on constraint satisfaction and extraction quality (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents, full S1 constraints). $k{=}1$ corresponds to greedy decoding.}
\label{tab:beam-ablation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rcccc@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
1 (greedy) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
2          & 0.35 & 4.12 & 31.54 & \textbf{8.75} \\
4          & \textbf{0}    & 0.53 & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.

$^\dagger$Greedy baselines from 998-document full evaluations; beam results on 50-document subsets due to compute constraints. $^*$Not a matched comparison; sample-level variance may account for minor F1 differences.

Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
Wall-clock overhead is modest; \texttt{early\_stopping} terminates generation once all beams produce a complete sequence, limiting the additional compute to partial-sequence exploration rather than full-length replication.
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

1	\section{Extended Related Work}
2	\label{app:related_work}
3	
4	% ===========================================================================
5	% Paradigm 1: Grammar-Constrained Decoding
6	% ===========================================================================
7	\paragraph{Grammar-Constrained Decoding.}
8	Recent work has established efficient algorithms for restricting LLM outputs to conform to context-free grammars, making grammar-constrained decoding the de facto standard for obtaining structured output from language models.
9	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar} partitions the vocabulary into context-independent and context-dependent tokens and maintains persistent pushdown automata across decoding steps, achieving up to 100$\times$ speedup over prior CFG-constrained decoding methods.
10	Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines} reformulates constrained generation as finite-state machine transitions with offline vocabulary indexing, enabling efficient enforcement of regular-expression and JSON-schema constraints without runtime overhead per token.
11	LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql} introduces a declarative query language that compiles type, length, and regex constraints into token-level masks, providing a programmable interface for specifying multi-variable output structures.
12	These systems ensure that every generated token belongs to a grammar-valid continuation, but they do not address the \emph{distribution distortion} introduced by naive token masking.
13	A parallel line of work tackles this problem directly: DOMINO~\cite{beurer-kellner2024domino} minimizes distributional divergence during CFG enforcement by formulating mask selection as an optimization problem, and ASAp~\cite{park2024grammar} provides a provably unbiased sampling algorithm that preserves the original LM distribution under grammar constraints.
14	Together, these advances have made grammar-constrained decoding both fast and statistically principled, establishing a robust foundation for structured generation.
15	However, all of these methods operate exclusively at the syntactic level---they ensure format validity (e.g., well-formed JSON, valid enum values) but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints such as ontology domain/range rules that depend on previously generated content.
16	This syntactic-only limitation motivates OntoCoDec's semantic extension: our grammar layer builds on XGrammar for structural (JSON schema and enum) constraints, while a second semantic layer enforces relational type constraints that are inherently beyond the expressive power of context-free grammars.
17	
18	% ===========================================================================
19	% Paradigm 1.5: Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code
20	% ===========================================================================
21	\paragraph{Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code.}
22	In programming-language generation, constrained decoding has been extended beyond syntax to enforce semantic properties such as type correctness, demonstrating that richer-than-CFG constraints can be compiled into token-level filtering.
23	In the text-to-SQL domain, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} maintains an incremental SQL parsing state that rejects tokens violating syntax or referencing non-existent database columns at each decoding step, achieving state-of-the-art results on Spider and CoSQL without modifying model weights.
24	While mechanistically similar to OntoCoDec's token-level filtering, PICARD operates over a \emph{fixed, fully enumerated} schema---database table and column names known before decoding begins.
25	In contrast, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated \emph{during} generation as entity spans are extracted from free text, requiring constraint sets that evolve with the decoding prefix---a fundamental distinction between querying a known schema and extracting from unstructured text.
26	Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} pioneers Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD), which enforces syntax, type, and scope constraints simultaneously during code generation from pre-trained LMs without fine-tuning, establishing that semantic constraints can be expressed as dynamic token masks conditioned on the generation prefix.
27	MGD~\cite{mgd_neurips2023} uses static-analysis monitors to perform incremental type checking at decode time, enabling SantaCoder-1.1B to outperform text-davinci-003 on repository-level code completion by ensuring that every generated identifier is type-correct with respect to the surrounding code context.
28	Most recently, \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems---including generic types and subtyping---into prefix automata for token-level logits masking, reducing compilation errors by over 50\%.
29	This last system is the closest mechanistic analog to OntoCoDec, applying the same ``type system $\to$ automaton $\to$ logits mask'' pipeline, though in a fundamentally different domain.
30	The key technical difference lies in the constraint structure: programming-language type systems feature deep subtyping hierarchies and parametric polymorphism, whereas IE ontology axioms specify flat domain/range sets---a relation $R$ accepts head entities from set $\mathcal{D}(R)$ and tail entities from set $\mathcal{R}(R)$, with no subtype chains.
31	Conversely, IE introduces a challenge absent in code generation: the constraint target (entity type) must be inferred from free-text spans rather than read from declared type annotations, requiring a stateful entity registry that tracks extracted types during autoregressive generation.
32	These methods collectively demonstrate that semantic (type) constraints at decode time are both feasible and highly effective, but exclusively in the code domain where type systems are formally specified.
33	OntoCoDec is the first to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontology axioms---including domain/range constraints---into token-level decoding masks for information extraction, migrating the type-constrained decoding paradigm from code generation to IE.
34	
35	% ===========================================================================
36	% Paradigm 2: Vocabulary/Type-Constrained Generation
37	% ===========================================================================
38	\paragraph{Vocabulary and Type-Constrained Generation.}
39	The idea of enforcing entity-type compatibility constraints for information extraction dates back to pre-neural methods.
40	\citet{roth_yih_2004} formulate joint entity and relation identification as an integer linear program (ILP) that enforces type constraints---e.g., \textsc{Emp-Org} only between \textsc{Per} and \textsc{Org} entities---establishing the foundational principle that relational type compatibility should be a hard constraint, not a soft preference learned from data.
41	In the autoregressive era, GENRE~\cite{decao2021genre} pioneers trie-based constrained beam search for autoregressive entity retrieval, restricting each decoding step to tokens consistent with valid entity names from a predefined catalog.
42	GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie} extends this approach to end-to-end information extraction with state-based constraints that enforce valid triple structures, achieving strong performance on closed-world knowledge base population, though it requires task-specific fine-tuning on the target schema.
43	AdaKGC~\cite{adakgc_emnlp2023} introduces schema-constrained dynamic decoding with trie-based prefix trees that adapt to the target schema, enforcing that generated entity and relation names belong to a predefined inventory---a vocabulary-level constraint that ensures name validity but does not verify type compatibility between a relation and its arguments.
44	GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} provides a unified grammar-constrained decoding framework for structured NLP tasks including IE, introducing input-dependent grammars that adapt constraints based on the source text---the closest precursor to OntoCoDec in applying logits masking to IE, though limited to syntactic constraints.
45	NeuroLogic Decoding~\cite{lu2021neurologic} expresses lexical inclusion and exclusion constraints as predicate logic formulas enforced during beam search, offering a general mechanism for token-level control that can encode vocabulary membership but not relational type rules.
46	These approaches constrain \emph{which tokens} can appear (vocabulary membership) but not \emph{which type combinations} are valid for a given relation.
47	OntoCoDec's semantic layer enforces relational constraints---e.g., that the head entity of relation $R$ must belong to type set $\mathcal{D}(R)$---which cannot be expressed as static vocabulary restrictions because the valid set depends on the relation type generated earlier in the same sequence.
48	While Roth \& Yih's ILP formulation shares the same type-compatibility motivation, it operates as a post-hoc reranker over discrete candidates; OntoCoDec integrates enforcement directly into autoregressive decoding, preventing violations rather than filtering them.
49	
50	% ===========================================================================
51	% Paradigm 3: Structural Constraints for IE
52	% ===========================================================================
53	\paragraph{Structural Constraints via Training and Prompting.}
54	An orthogonal approach encodes IE output structure through model training or prompt design rather than decoding-time enforcement, relying on learned representations to produce schema-compliant outputs.
55	UIE~\cite{lu2022uie} defines a Structured Extraction Language and trains a unified text-to-structure model across 13 IE datasets, relying on large-scale pre-training to internalize output format constraints.
56	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} expresses annotation guidelines as Python dataclass definitions and fine-tunes Code-LLaMA to generate typed code, achieving strong zero-shot transfer to unseen IE schemas by leveraging the implicit type structure of programming languages.
57	KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} takes this further by encoding 29K entity types from Wikidata as a Python class hierarchy, training a Code-LLM to generate structured extraction code that implicitly respects type inheritance---the most comprehensive schema-as-code approach to date.
58	CodeIE~\cite{li2023codeie} similarly reformulates IE as code generation, leveraging the structural regularity of programming languages to reduce output format errors.
59	ADELIE~\cite{qi2024adelie} uses SFT and DPO to align LLMs on IE tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source models while preserving general capabilities, though compliance with ontological constraints remains a learned soft preference rather than a guarantee.
60	In the supervised setting, joint entity-relation architectures such as SpERT~\cite{eberts2020spert} and PFN~\cite{yan2021pfn} enforce type consistency implicitly through shared representations: SpERT classifies entity spans and relation pairs in a single BERT pass with span-level negative sampling, while PFN decomposes feature encoding into entity-specific, relation-specific, and shared partitions via gating mechanisms.
61	These models achieve strong performance but are limited to fixed, predefined schemas and cannot generalize to unseen ontologies without retraining---precisely the zero-shot, ontology-portable scenario that OntoCoDec targets.
62	EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} applies Answer Set Programming (ASP) constraints during decoding of joint entity-relation extraction models, enforcing structural type compatibility at generation time---a decoding-time approach, though with model-specific, manually authored constraints rather than ontology-driven compilation.
63	Training-based methods provide \emph{soft} structural guidance---the model learns to prefer valid outputs but cannot guarantee compliance at inference time, as demonstrated by non-trivial violation rates even in fine-tuned systems.
64	Importantly, training-based and decoding-time approaches are complementary rather than competing: a system like GoLLIE could be combined with OntoCoDec's constraint layers, using fine-tuning to maximize the probability of valid outputs while decoding-time enforcement eliminates residual violations.
65	OntoCoDec provides \emph{hard} decoding-time enforcement that is training-free, automatically compiled from ontology schemas, and composable with any of these training-based approaches.
66	
67	% ===========================================================================
68	% Paradigm 4: Type-Checking / Ontology Validation
69	% ===========================================================================
70	\paragraph{Post-hoc Ontology Validation.}
71	Rather than constraining generation, several methods validate LLM outputs against ontological rules after generation, applying a detect-then-fix paradigm.
72	ODKE+~\cite{khorshidi2025odke} dynamically generates ontology snippets containing domain/range constraints as prompt context, achieving 98.8\% precision across 195 predicates at web scale---but constraint adherence relies on prompt-level guidance, not enforcement, leaving residual violations unaddressed.
73	SPIRES/OntoGPT~\cite{spires_2024} provides an ontology-based extraction framework that grounds LLM outputs against OBO ontologies post-generation, validating extracted entities and relations through ontology lookup and correcting mismatches in a second pass---representing the prompt-then-validate paradigm in the biomedical domain.
74	OntoLogX~\cite{ontologx_2025} applies SHACL validation to LLM-generated knowledge graphs, iteratively re-prompting the LLM to correct constraint violations and reducing them by approximately 10$\times$ across multiple correction rounds---demonstrating the detect-then-fix paradigm's effectiveness but also its inherent multi-pass cost.
75	\citet{upadhyay2023openie} inject entity-type knowledge as constraints into Open IE via both constrained inference and constraint-aware training, improving F1 by 29\% on CaRB, though their constrained inference operates over a discrete candidate set rather than during autoregressive generation.
76	\citet{regino2025kgcurator} propose a multi-stage LLM pipeline for validating RDF triple insertions against RDFS domain/range constraints, where each validation step requires a separate LLM call---effective but computationally expensive at scale.
77	RELATE~\cite{olasunkanmi2025relate} addresses the alignment gap between LLM-extracted biomedical relations and standardized ontology predicates through a three-stage pipeline: ontology preprocessing with predicate embeddings, similarity-based retrieval via SapBERT, and LLM-based reranking with negation handling, achieving 94\% accuracy@10 on ChemProt.
78	While RELATE demonstrates effective ontology grounding for relation extraction, its constraints are applied \emph{post-extraction} through retrieval and reranking rather than during generation, and it requires domain-specific embedding models trained on biomedical corpora.
79	OntoCoDec enforces ontology constraints \emph{during} autoregressive decoding and requires no additional trained components beyond the base LLM.
80	Concurrently, \citet{zhou2026ontologytools} compile OWL ontologies into executable tool interfaces within The World Avatar framework, requiring LLM agents to invoke ontology-aware tools that enforce semantic constraints during knowledge graph construction from scientific text.
81	This ``ontology-to-tools'' approach shares OntoCoDec's philosophy of compiling formal ontological knowledge into runtime enforcement mechanisms, but operates at the tool-call level (constraining which API functions the agent invokes) rather than at the token level (constraining which tokens the decoder produces), and requires an agentic multi-step workflow rather than single-pass autoregressive generation.
82	\citet{ekaw2024_ontology_beam} introduce ontology-constrained beam scoring for clinical summarization, applying soft biases (not hard masks) during beam search to steer outputs toward ontology-compliant terms---a middle ground between unconstrained generation and hard enforcement that reduces but cannot eliminate violations.
83	Post-hoc validation detects violations after generation, requiring rejection or correction cycles that waste compute---in our setting, 15.37\% of generated triples contain domain/range violations under unconstrained decoding, representing substantial wasted generation effort.
84	OntoCoDec \emph{prevents} violations during decoding, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives rather than discarding invalid outputs, with only marginal overhead from logits masking compared to the cost of regenerating or correcting violated triples.
85	Soft-constraint approaches such as ontology-weighted beam scoring reduce violation frequency but cannot eliminate it, whereas OntoCoDec substantially reduces violations (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45--90\% on DocRED depending on model).
86	
87	% ===========================================================================
88	% Paradigm 5: Constrained Decoding Quality Concerns
89	% ===========================================================================
90	\paragraph{Quality Impact of Constrained Decoding.}
91	A growing body of work raises concerns that constrained decoding degrades LLM generation quality, particularly for reasoning-intensive tasks where format enforcement interferes with chain-of-thought processes.
92	\citet{tam2024letmespeak} conduct a comprehensive evaluation showing that rigid format constraints (JSON, XML) harm performance on math and multi-hop QA benchmarks but \emph{benefit} classification-style tasks such as slot filling---a distinction directly relevant to IE, which is fundamentally an extraction (classification-like) task rather than a reasoning task.
93	CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane} provides theoretical analysis of why restricting outputs to narrow grammars suppresses chain-of-thought reasoning by eliminating intermediate reasoning tokens, and proposes an alternating strategy between unconstrained reasoning phases and constrained output phases to mitigate this effect.
94	\citet{schall2025hiddencost} conduct a systematic study across 11 models and multiple benchmarks, finding 10--30\% semantic correctness degradation on reasoning tasks under structural constraints, with larger models showing greater absolute degradation.
95	\citet{zhou2026snowballing} identify ``structure snowballing''---a failure mode where format compliance cognitive load traps models in repetitive structural patterns rather than improving reasoning during self-correction iterations.
96	These findings establish a legitimate concern for constrained decoding in reasoning-heavy applications.
97	However, information extraction occupies a fundamentally different regime: the model extracts entities and relations from input text rather than generating novel reasoning chains, and \citet{tam2024letmespeak}'s own results show that extraction-style tasks are robust to---or even benefit from---format constraints.
98	OntoCoDec addresses this concern empirically: domain/range violations decrease by 94\% on SciERC (15.37\%$\to$0.93\%) and 45--90\% on DocRED across two models, with F1-neutral impact on SciERC ($+$0.13pp, $p{=}0.58$) and significant R-F1 gains on DocRED (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$).

\section{Extended Related Work}
\label{app:related_work}

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 1: Grammar-Constrained Decoding
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Grammar-Constrained Decoding.}
Recent work has established efficient algorithms for restricting LLM outputs to conform to context-free grammars, making grammar-constrained decoding the de facto standard for obtaining structured output from language models.
XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar} partitions the vocabulary into context-independent and context-dependent tokens and maintains persistent pushdown automata across decoding steps, achieving up to 100$\times$ speedup over prior CFG-constrained decoding methods.
Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines} reformulates constrained generation as finite-state machine transitions with offline vocabulary indexing, enabling efficient enforcement of regular-expression and JSON-schema constraints without runtime overhead per token.
LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql} introduces a declarative query language that compiles type, length, and regex constraints into token-level masks, providing a programmable interface for specifying multi-variable output structures.
These systems ensure that every generated token belongs to a grammar-valid continuation, but they do not address the \emph{distribution distortion} introduced by naive token masking.
A parallel line of work tackles this problem directly: DOMINO~\cite{beurer-kellner2024domino} minimizes distributional divergence during CFG enforcement by formulating mask selection as an optimization problem, and ASAp~\cite{park2024grammar} provides a provably unbiased sampling algorithm that preserves the original LM distribution under grammar constraints.
Together, these advances have made grammar-constrained decoding both fast and statistically principled, establishing a robust foundation for structured generation.
However, all of these methods operate exclusively at the syntactic level---they ensure format validity (e.g., well-formed JSON, valid enum values) but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints such as ontology domain/range rules that depend on previously generated content.
This syntactic-only limitation motivates OntoCoDec's semantic extension: our grammar layer builds on XGrammar for structural (JSON schema and enum) constraints, while a second semantic layer enforces relational type constraints that are inherently beyond the expressive power of context-free grammars.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 1.5: Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code.}
In programming-language generation, constrained decoding has been extended beyond syntax to enforce semantic properties such as type correctness, demonstrating that richer-than-CFG constraints can be compiled into token-level filtering.
In the text-to-SQL domain, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} maintains an incremental SQL parsing state that rejects tokens violating syntax or referencing non-existent database columns at each decoding step, achieving state-of-the-art results on Spider and CoSQL without modifying model weights.
While mechanistically similar to OntoCoDec's token-level filtering, PICARD operates over a \emph{fixed, fully enumerated} schema---database table and column names known before decoding begins.
In contrast, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated \emph{during} generation as entity spans are extracted from free text, requiring constraint sets that evolve with the decoding prefix---a fundamental distinction between querying a known schema and extracting from unstructured text.
Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} pioneers Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD), which enforces syntax, type, and scope constraints simultaneously during code generation from pre-trained LMs without fine-tuning, establishing that semantic constraints can be expressed as dynamic token masks conditioned on the generation prefix.
MGD~\cite{mgd_neurips2023} uses static-analysis monitors to perform incremental type checking at decode time, enabling SantaCoder-1.1B to outperform text-davinci-003 on repository-level code completion by ensuring that every generated identifier is type-correct with respect to the surrounding code context.
Most recently, \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems---including generic types and subtyping---into prefix automata for token-level logits masking, reducing compilation errors by over 50\%.
This last system is the closest mechanistic analog to OntoCoDec, applying the same ``type system $\to$ automaton $\to$ logits mask'' pipeline, though in a fundamentally different domain.
The key technical difference lies in the constraint structure: programming-language type systems feature deep subtyping hierarchies and parametric polymorphism, whereas IE ontology axioms specify flat domain/range sets---a relation $R$ accepts head entities from set $\mathcal{D}(R)$ and tail entities from set $\mathcal{R}(R)$, with no subtype chains.
Conversely, IE introduces a challenge absent in code generation: the constraint target (entity type) must be inferred from free-text spans rather than read from declared type annotations, requiring a stateful entity registry that tracks extracted types during autoregressive generation.
These methods collectively demonstrate that semantic (type) constraints at decode time are both feasible and highly effective, but exclusively in the code domain where type systems are formally specified.
OntoCoDec is the first to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontology axioms---including domain/range constraints---into token-level decoding masks for information extraction, migrating the type-constrained decoding paradigm from code generation to IE.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 2: Vocabulary/Type-Constrained Generation
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Vocabulary and Type-Constrained Generation.}
The idea of enforcing entity-type compatibility constraints for information extraction dates back to pre-neural methods.
\citet{roth_yih_2004} formulate joint entity and relation identification as an integer linear program (ILP) that enforces type constraints---e.g., \textsc{Emp-Org} only between \textsc{Per} and \textsc{Org} entities---establishing the foundational principle that relational type compatibility should be a hard constraint, not a soft preference learned from data.
In the autoregressive era, GENRE~\cite{decao2021genre} pioneers trie-based constrained beam search for autoregressive entity retrieval, restricting each decoding step to tokens consistent with valid entity names from a predefined catalog.
GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie} extends this approach to end-to-end information extraction with state-based constraints that enforce valid triple structures, achieving strong performance on closed-world knowledge base population, though it requires task-specific fine-tuning on the target schema.
AdaKGC~\cite{adakgc_emnlp2023} introduces schema-constrained dynamic decoding with trie-based prefix trees that adapt to the target schema, enforcing that generated entity and relation names belong to a predefined inventory---a vocabulary-level constraint that ensures name validity but does not verify type compatibility between a relation and its arguments.
GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} provides a unified grammar-constrained decoding framework for structured NLP tasks including IE, introducing input-dependent grammars that adapt constraints based on the source text---the closest precursor to OntoCoDec in applying logits masking to IE, though limited to syntactic constraints.
NeuroLogic Decoding~\cite{lu2021neurologic} expresses lexical inclusion and exclusion constraints as predicate logic formulas enforced during beam search, offering a general mechanism for token-level control that can encode vocabulary membership but not relational type rules.
These approaches constrain \emph{which tokens} can appear (vocabulary membership) but not \emph{which type combinations} are valid for a given relation.
OntoCoDec's semantic layer enforces relational constraints---e.g., that the head entity of relation $R$ must belong to type set $\mathcal{D}(R)$---which cannot be expressed as static vocabulary restrictions because the valid set depends on the relation type generated earlier in the same sequence.
While Roth \& Yih's ILP formulation shares the same type-compatibility motivation, it operates as a post-hoc reranker over discrete candidates; OntoCoDec integrates enforcement directly into autoregressive decoding, preventing violations rather than filtering them.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 3: Structural Constraints for IE
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Structural Constraints via Training and Prompting.}
An orthogonal approach encodes IE output structure through model training or prompt design rather than decoding-time enforcement, relying on learned representations to produce schema-compliant outputs.
UIE~\cite{lu2022uie} defines a Structured Extraction Language and trains a unified text-to-structure model across 13 IE datasets, relying on large-scale pre-training to internalize output format constraints.
GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} expresses annotation guidelines as Python dataclass definitions and fine-tunes Code-LLaMA to generate typed code, achieving strong zero-shot transfer to unseen IE schemas by leveraging the implicit type structure of programming languages.
KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} takes this further by encoding 29K entity types from Wikidata as a Python class hierarchy, training a Code-LLM to generate structured extraction code that implicitly respects type inheritance---the most comprehensive schema-as-code approach to date.
CodeIE~\cite{li2023codeie} similarly reformulates IE as code generation, leveraging the structural regularity of programming languages to reduce output format errors.
ADELIE~\cite{qi2024adelie} uses SFT and DPO to align LLMs on IE tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source models while preserving general capabilities, though compliance with ontological constraints remains a learned soft preference rather than a guarantee.
In the supervised setting, joint entity-relation architectures such as SpERT~\cite{eberts2020spert} and PFN~\cite{yan2021pfn} enforce type consistency implicitly through shared representations: SpERT classifies entity spans and relation pairs in a single BERT pass with span-level negative sampling, while PFN decomposes feature encoding into entity-specific, relation-specific, and shared partitions via gating mechanisms.
These models achieve strong performance but are limited to fixed, predefined schemas and cannot generalize to unseen ontologies without retraining---precisely the zero-shot, ontology-portable scenario that OntoCoDec targets.
EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} applies Answer Set Programming (ASP) constraints during decoding of joint entity-relation extraction models, enforcing structural type compatibility at generation time---a decoding-time approach, though with model-specific, manually authored constraints rather than ontology-driven compilation.
Training-based methods provide \emph{soft} structural guidance---the model learns to prefer valid outputs but cannot guarantee compliance at inference time, as demonstrated by non-trivial violation rates even in fine-tuned systems.
Importantly, training-based and decoding-time approaches are complementary rather than competing: a system like GoLLIE could be combined with OntoCoDec's constraint layers, using fine-tuning to maximize the probability of valid outputs while decoding-time enforcement eliminates residual violations.
OntoCoDec provides \emph{hard} decoding-time enforcement that is training-free, automatically compiled from ontology schemas, and composable with any of these training-based approaches.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 4: Type-Checking / Ontology Validation
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Post-hoc Ontology Validation.}
Rather than constraining generation, several methods validate LLM outputs against ontological rules after generation, applying a detect-then-fix paradigm.
ODKE+~\cite{khorshidi2025odke} dynamically generates ontology snippets containing domain/range constraints as prompt context, achieving 98.8\% precision across 195 predicates at web scale---but constraint adherence relies on prompt-level guidance, not enforcement, leaving residual violations unaddressed.
SPIRES/OntoGPT~\cite{spires_2024} provides an ontology-based extraction framework that grounds LLM outputs against OBO ontologies post-generation, validating extracted entities and relations through ontology lookup and correcting mismatches in a second pass---representing the prompt-then-validate paradigm in the biomedical domain.
OntoLogX~\cite{ontologx_2025} applies SHACL validation to LLM-generated knowledge graphs, iteratively re-prompting the LLM to correct constraint violations and reducing them by approximately 10$\times$ across multiple correction rounds---demonstrating the detect-then-fix paradigm's effectiveness but also its inherent multi-pass cost.
\citet{upadhyay2023openie} inject entity-type knowledge as constraints into Open IE via both constrained inference and constraint-aware training, improving F1 by 29\% on CaRB, though their constrained inference operates over a discrete candidate set rather than during autoregressive generation.
\citet{regino2025kgcurator} propose a multi-stage LLM pipeline for validating RDF triple insertions against RDFS domain/range constraints, where each validation step requires a separate LLM call---effective but computationally expensive at scale.
RELATE~\cite{olasunkanmi2025relate} addresses the alignment gap between LLM-extracted biomedical relations and standardized ontology predicates through a three-stage pipeline: ontology preprocessing with predicate embeddings, similarity-based retrieval via SapBERT, and LLM-based reranking with negation handling, achieving 94\% accuracy@10 on ChemProt.
While RELATE demonstrates effective ontology grounding for relation extraction, its constraints are applied \emph{post-extraction} through retrieval and reranking rather than during generation, and it requires domain-specific embedding models trained on biomedical corpora.
OntoCoDec enforces ontology constraints \emph{during} autoregressive decoding and requires no additional trained components beyond the base LLM.
Concurrently, \citet{zhou2026ontologytools} compile OWL ontologies into executable tool interfaces within The World Avatar framework, requiring LLM agents to invoke ontology-aware tools that enforce semantic constraints during knowledge graph construction from scientific text.
This ``ontology-to-tools'' approach shares OntoCoDec's philosophy of compiling formal ontological knowledge into runtime enforcement mechanisms, but operates at the tool-call level (constraining which API functions the agent invokes) rather than at the token level (constraining which tokens the decoder produces), and requires an agentic multi-step workflow rather than single-pass autoregressive generation.
\citet{ekaw2024_ontology_beam} introduce ontology-constrained beam scoring for clinical summarization, applying soft biases (not hard masks) during beam search to steer outputs toward ontology-compliant terms---a middle ground between unconstrained generation and hard enforcement that reduces but cannot eliminate violations.
Post-hoc validation detects violations after generation, requiring rejection or correction cycles that waste compute---in our setting, 15.37\% of generated triples contain domain/range violations under unconstrained decoding, representing substantial wasted generation effort.
OntoCoDec \emph{prevents} violations during decoding, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives rather than discarding invalid outputs, with only marginal overhead from logits masking compared to the cost of regenerating or correcting violated triples.
Soft-constraint approaches such as ontology-weighted beam scoring reduce violation frequency but cannot eliminate it, whereas OntoCoDec substantially reduces violations (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45--90\% on DocRED depending on model).

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 5: Constrained Decoding Quality Concerns
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Quality Impact of Constrained Decoding.}
A growing body of work raises concerns that constrained decoding degrades LLM generation quality, particularly for reasoning-intensive tasks where format enforcement interferes with chain-of-thought processes.
\citet{tam2024letmespeak} conduct a comprehensive evaluation showing that rigid format constraints (JSON, XML) harm performance on math and multi-hop QA benchmarks but \emph{benefit} classification-style tasks such as slot filling---a distinction directly relevant to IE, which is fundamentally an extraction (classification-like) task rather than a reasoning task.
CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane} provides theoretical analysis of why restricting outputs to narrow grammars suppresses chain-of-thought reasoning by eliminating intermediate reasoning tokens, and proposes an alternating strategy between unconstrained reasoning phases and constrained output phases to mitigate this effect.
\citet{schall2025hiddencost} conduct a systematic study across 11 models and multiple benchmarks, finding 10--30\% semantic correctness degradation on reasoning tasks under structural constraints, with larger models showing greater absolute degradation.
\citet{zhou2026snowballing} identify ``structure snowballing''---a failure mode where format compliance cognitive load traps models in repetitive structural patterns rather than improving reasoning during self-correction iterations.
These findings establish a legitimate concern for constrained decoding in reasoning-heavy applications.
However, information extraction occupies a fundamentally different regime: the model extracts entities and relations from input text rather than generating novel reasoning chains, and \citet{tam2024letmespeak}'s own results show that extraction-style tasks are robust to---or even benefit from---format constraints.
OntoCoDec addresses this concern empirically: domain/range violations decrease by 94\% on SciERC (15.37\%$\to$0.93\%) and 45--90\% on DocRED across two models, with F1-neutral impact on SciERC ($+$0.13pp, $p{=}0.58$) and significant R-F1 gains on DocRED (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$).
Critically, OntoCoDec's constraints target only type tokens (entity types, relation labels), leaving free-text spans---entity surface forms and their boundaries---entirely unconstrained, which minimizes the distribution distortion that causes quality degradation in reasoning tasks.
A two-pass variant (S2), explored in ablation (Section~5), separates extraction and constraint enforcement into distinct passes, analogous to CRANE's alternating strategy; however, our primary single-pass approach already avoids reasoning interference by constraining only type tokens while leaving free-text spans unconstrained.

% ===========================================================================
% Our Approach
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Our Approach.}
OntoCoDec occupies a unique position in this landscape: it is the first system to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontology schemas---including domain/range axioms---into token-level semantic masks, extending grammar-constrained decoding from syntactic to semantic enforcement without manually authored rules.
Unlike vocabulary-constrained methods that restrict individual tokens to a fixed set, OntoCoDec enforces \emph{cross-field relational constraints} through a stateful entity registry that tracks extracted types during autoregressive generation, enabling dynamic constraint evaluation that depends on previously decoded content.
This approach is orthogonal to supervised IE methods and applicable to any autoregressive LM without model modification or additional training.
Unlike training-based IE systems, OntoCoDec is training-free and substantially reduces type violations at inference time (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45--90\% on DocRED); unlike post-hoc validation, it prevents violations rather than detecting them, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives with significant R-F1 gains on DocRED ($p \leq 0.013$) and F1-neutral impact on SciERC.
The two constraint layers---grammar (structural) and semantic (relational)---compose via bitwise AND with an enabling dependency: the grammar layer ensures every generated type token belongs to the valid vocabulary, which enables the semantic layer to look up and enforce domain/range rules for that type.

1	# Rebuttal Draft v2 — Response to Reviewer (Group C)
2	
3	---
4	
5	## Q1: CF and DR Weight / Interaction
6	
7	**Concern**: The reviewer asks how CF (Cross-Field consistency violations) and DR (Domain-Range violations) are weighted and whether they trade off against each other.
8	
9	**Response**:
10	CF and DR measure fundamentally different properties and should not be combined into a single weighted metric. DR measures ontological constraint violations (whether entity-type pairs are valid for a given relation), while CF measures cross-field consistency (whether head/tail entities referenced in a relation triple match previously declared entities). They operate on orthogonal axes of schema compliance.
11	
12	Table 5 (ablation) reports CF and DR separately precisely to expose the trade-off landscape. The key finding: CF rises when the semantic layer is active (full_s1: CF=9.90% on SciERC) because CF is a *byproduct* of the constraint fallback mechanism, not an independent optimization target. When the semantic layer's bitwise AND of grammar mask and domain-range mask produces an empty set (no token simultaneously satisfies both constraints), the system falls back to grammar-only decoding for that token position. This fallback may produce an entity name that is grammatically valid but inconsistent with previously generated fields — hence CF. The fallback design prioritizes generating *some* valid output over blocking generation entirely.
13	
14	Crucially, DR reduction (15.37% → 0.93% on SciERC, a 93.9% relative reduction) vastly outweighs the CF increase (+9.82pp), and CF violations are inherently less severe: they represent internal naming inconsistencies that downstream systems can resolve via string matching, whereas DR violations represent fundamentally invalid semantic assertions.
15	
16	Furthermore, on SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B), beam search ($k$=4) largely resolves the CF trade-off: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, reducing CF from 9.90% to 0.53% while eliminating all residual DR (0.93%→0%). This indicates that CF elevation under greedy decoding is an artifact of single-path search encountering grammar∩semantic=∅ conflicts, not a fundamental limitation of the constraint design.
17	
18	**Action**: Add a clarifying footnote in Section 5 explaining that CF is a constraint-fallback artifact, not an independent error mode to be minimized jointly with DR.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Q2: Quality of Grammar-Layer Replacements for OOV Relations
23	
24	**Concern**: The reviewer questions whether the grammar layer's replacement of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) relation names produces semantically meaningful outputs.
25	
26	**Response**:
27	This is precisely the limitation that motivates the semantic constraint layer. In the DocRED zero-shot unconstrained setting, we observe **5,261 triples with OOV relation names** (out of 2,038 unique OOV strings). The grammar layer replaces 4,357 of these with in-vocabulary names, but **36.6% (1,594) of replacements introduce new DR violations**. This occurs because XGrammar performs token-level CFG steering — it selects the nearest *syntactically* valid continuation based on token-prefix matching, with no semantic awareness.
28	
29	We identify three failure modes:
30	
31	1. **Token-prefix collisions**: "opponent" → "operator" (both share prefix "op"); "peaked at" → "performer" (share "pe"). These produce semantically absurd triples (e.g., a cricketer "operates" a country).
32	
33	2. **Ontology gaps**: "population", "instrument" have no valid DocRED equivalent. Any grammar-forced replacement is necessarily wrong (e.g., "population" → "has part", asserting a numeric value is a constituent part of a county).
34	
35	3. **Silent semantic errors**: "available on" → "operator" passes type-checking (ORG→ORG is valid for P137) but reverses the semantic direction, producing undetectable errors at the type level.
36	
37	These findings directly justify the two-layer architecture: the grammar layer guarantees *syntactic* schema validity (eliminating ET and RV violations entirely), while the semantic layer is needed to enforce *relational* validity that token-level matching cannot achieve.
38	
39	**Action**: Add a brief discussion in Section 4.3 with 2-3 representative replacement examples and aggregate statistics (36.6% DR-inducing rate).
40	
41	---
42	
43	## Q3: Is Grammar Redundant Under Fine-Tuning?
44	
45	**Concern**: The reviewer suggests that fine-tuned models may not need the grammar constraint layer at all.
46	
47	**Response**:
48	The FT ablation confirms that grammar constraints are indeed *operationally redundant* for ET and RV in fine-tuned models — both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B produce zero ET violations and near-zero RV violations without constraints after fine-tuning. However, the grammar layer serves two essential roles even in the FT regime:
49	
50	**Role 1: Eliminating residual RV.** On DocRED, FT-Qwen unconstrained still shows RV=0.27% and FT-Llama shows RV=0.15%. Grammar-only mode reduces both to RV=0% (Tables 1-2 of the FT ablation). While small in absolute terms, this guarantees zero vocabulary violations — a hard requirement for downstream knowledge graph construction.
51	
52	**Role 2: Enabling the semantic layer.** The semantic layer's domain-range enforcement operates by looking up the generated relation name in the ontology to retrieve valid (head_type, tail_type) pairs. If the relation name is OOV (not in vocabulary), the lookup fails and no constraint can be applied. Grammar ensures every generated relation name is in-vocabulary, thereby enabling the semantic layer to function. Without grammar, the semantic-only mode on DocRED FT still shows RV=0.23% (Qwen) / 0.15% (Llama) — these represent cases where the semantic layer cannot enforce DR constraints because it cannot resolve the relation name.
53	
54	The ablation data confirms the complementarity: Semantic-only reduces DR by 39–72% across all four model×dataset settings, but the full system (grammar + semantic) achieves the lowest DR in all cases (0–0.20%), because the grammar layer's guarantee of valid relation names enables complete semantic enforcement.
55	
56	**Action**: Add a sentence in Section 6.2 explicitly noting that grammar's FT-regime role is as an enabling dependency for the semantic layer rather than as an independent violation reducer.
57	
58	---
59	
60	## Q4: R² Generalizability and Mistral as Outlier
61	
62	**Concern**: The reviewer questions whether the dual-factor regression (R²=0.886) generalizes beyond the four calibrated data points, particularly given Mistral's deviation.
63	
64	**Response**:
65	We use a **dual-factor model** regressing `residual_DR ~ τ̄ × RV_baseline` (schema tightness multiplied by the model's relation vocabulary violation baseline). On n=4 calibrated points (Qwen + Llama, each on SciERC and DocRED), this model achieves **R² = 0.886**, accurately predicting the residual DR that remains after semantic constraint application. We acknowledge this is descriptive rather than predictive at the current sample size — it characterizes the relationship between schema tightness, vocabulary confusion, and residual DR for models that have been properly calibrated to the target schema.
66	
67	Mistral constitutes a **boundary condition** that reveals a qualitatively different error mode. On SciERC, Mistral shows RV=0% (no vocabulary confusion) yet residual DR=13.4%. This disconnect arises because Mistral's DR originates from **entity type misclassification** — it generates syntactically valid relation names but systematically assigns wrong entity types (e.g., labeling organizations as persons), producing type-pair violations that the dual-factor model (which captures vocabulary-confusion-driven DR) does not account for. We do not report a 6-point R² because Mistral is a catastrophic outlier driven by a mechanistically distinct error source, making the aggregate statistic uninformative.
68	
69	The dual-factor model's value is precisely in delineating *when* the semantic constraint layer is sufficient (calibrated models where DR stems from vocabulary confusion scaled by schema restrictiveness) versus *when* additional interventions are needed (models exhibiting systematic type misclassification). Mistral's deviation is thus a finding — it identifies entity type misclassification as a novel error mode that constrained decoding alone cannot address, motivating future work on type-aware decoding constraints.
70	
71	**Action**: Reframe the R² discussion in Section 5.4 as a "calibrated-model characterization" with the dual-factor formulation, and explicitly position Mistral as a boundary condition that reveals when grammar+semantic constraints are most impactful versus when a different error mechanism dominates.
72	
73	---
74	
75	## Q5: Fuzzy Matching Threshold Sensitivity
76	
77	**Concern**: The reviewer asks whether the fuzzy matching thresholds (Jaccard > 0.8, Levenshtein ≤ 2) were tuned on the evaluation data, potentially inflating reported metrics.
78	
79	**Response**:
80	The thresholds are **a priori constants**, not tuned parameters. Both values (Token Jaccard > 0.8, Levenshtein distance ≤ 2) are hardcoded identically across 6 evaluation files (`violation_checker.py`, `unified_f1_eval.py`, `compute_bootstrap_ci.py`, `posthoc_filter.py`, etc.) with no parameterized interface — no CLI argument, no config file, no sweep code exists. They represent standard NLP soft-matching defaults (0.8 Jaccard ≈ allow 1/5 token difference; ≤2 Levenshtein ≈ tolerate minor typos).
81	
82	More importantly, **fuzzy matching has negligible impact on reported results**:
83	
84	| Scope | Fuzzy match triggers | Total triples | Impact |
85	|-------|---------------------|---------------|--------|
86	| DocRED ZS unconstrained | 129 | 17,497 | 0.74% |
87	| All constrained modes (grammar/semantic/full) | **0** | — | **0%** |
88	| All FT experiments | **0** | — | **0%** |
89	| All SciERC experiments | **0** | — | **0%** |
90	
91	Fuzzy matching triggers *only* in DocRED zero-shot unconstrained mode (where the model occasionally generates near-miss relation names like "country" for P17). In all constrained decoding modes — which constitute the primary experimental claims — and in all fine-tuned models, the fuzzy match count is exactly zero. The strict-vs-fuzzy R_F1 difference is <0.1pp even in the one setting where it triggers.
92	
93	All main conclusions (DR reduction, layer complementarity, FT ablation findings) rest entirely on strict matching.
94	
95	**Action**: Add a footnote in Section 4.1 (Evaluation Protocol) stating that thresholds are fixed a priori constants and that fuzzy matching triggers in <1% of triples, exclusively in unconstrained baselines.
96	
97	---
98	
99	## Additional Points (for Author Response if space permits)
100	
101	### M7: Beam Search / Sampling Compatibility
102	
103	We have now validated constraint robustness under **nucleus sampling** (temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9) on full SciERC (551 docs) and a DocRED subset (114 docs).
104	
105	| Dataset | Decoding | ET% | RV% | DR% | CF% | E-F1 | R-F1 |

# Rebuttal Draft v2 — Response to Reviewer (Group C)

---

## Q1: CF and DR Weight / Interaction

**Concern**: The reviewer asks how CF (Cross-Field consistency violations) and DR (Domain-Range violations) are weighted and whether they trade off against each other.

**Response**:
CF and DR measure fundamentally different properties and should not be combined into a single weighted metric. DR measures ontological constraint violations (whether entity-type pairs are valid for a given relation), while CF measures cross-field consistency (whether head/tail entities referenced in a relation triple match previously declared entities). They operate on orthogonal axes of schema compliance.

Table 5 (ablation) reports CF and DR separately precisely to expose the trade-off landscape. The key finding: CF rises when the semantic layer is active (full_s1: CF=9.90% on SciERC) because CF is a *byproduct* of the constraint fallback mechanism, not an independent optimization target. When the semantic layer's bitwise AND of grammar mask and domain-range mask produces an empty set (no token simultaneously satisfies both constraints), the system falls back to grammar-only decoding for that token position. This fallback may produce an entity name that is grammatically valid but inconsistent with previously generated fields — hence CF. The fallback design prioritizes generating *some* valid output over blocking generation entirely.

Crucially, DR reduction (15.37% → 0.93% on SciERC, a 93.9% relative reduction) vastly outweighs the CF increase (+9.82pp), and CF violations are inherently less severe: they represent internal naming inconsistencies that downstream systems can resolve via string matching, whereas DR violations represent fundamentally invalid semantic assertions.

Furthermore, on SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B), beam search ($k$=4) largely resolves the CF trade-off: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, reducing CF from 9.90% to 0.53% while eliminating all residual DR (0.93%→0%). This indicates that CF elevation under greedy decoding is an artifact of single-path search encountering grammar∩semantic=∅ conflicts, not a fundamental limitation of the constraint design.

**Action**: Add a clarifying footnote in Section 5 explaining that CF is a constraint-fallback artifact, not an independent error mode to be minimized jointly with DR.

---

## Q2: Quality of Grammar-Layer Replacements for OOV Relations

**Concern**: The reviewer questions whether the grammar layer's replacement of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) relation names produces semantically meaningful outputs.

**Response**:
This is precisely the limitation that motivates the semantic constraint layer. In the DocRED zero-shot unconstrained setting, we observe **5,261 triples with OOV relation names** (out of 2,038 unique OOV strings). The grammar layer replaces 4,357 of these with in-vocabulary names, but **36.6% (1,594) of replacements introduce new DR violations**. This occurs because XGrammar performs token-level CFG steering — it selects the nearest *syntactically* valid continuation based on token-prefix matching, with no semantic awareness.

We identify three failure modes:

1. **Token-prefix collisions**: "opponent" → "operator" (both share prefix "op"); "peaked at" → "performer" (share "pe"). These produce semantically absurd triples (e.g., a cricketer "operates" a country).

2. **Ontology gaps**: "population", "instrument" have no valid DocRED equivalent. Any grammar-forced replacement is necessarily wrong (e.g., "population" → "has part", asserting a numeric value is a constituent part of a county).

3. **Silent semantic errors**: "available on" → "operator" passes type-checking (ORG→ORG is valid for P137) but reverses the semantic direction, producing undetectable errors at the type level.

These findings directly justify the two-layer architecture: the grammar layer guarantees *syntactic* schema validity (eliminating ET and RV violations entirely), while the semantic layer is needed to enforce *relational* validity that token-level matching cannot achieve.

**Action**: Add a brief discussion in Section 4.3 with 2-3 representative replacement examples and aggregate statistics (36.6% DR-inducing rate).

---

## Q3: Is Grammar Redundant Under Fine-Tuning?

**Concern**: The reviewer suggests that fine-tuned models may not need the grammar constraint layer at all.

**Response**:
The FT ablation confirms that grammar constraints are indeed *operationally redundant* for ET and RV in fine-tuned models — both Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B produce zero ET violations and near-zero RV violations without constraints after fine-tuning. However, the grammar layer serves two essential roles even in the FT regime:

**Role 1: Eliminating residual RV.** On DocRED, FT-Qwen unconstrained still shows RV=0.27% and FT-Llama shows RV=0.15%. Grammar-only mode reduces both to RV=0% (Tables 1-2 of the FT ablation). While small in absolute terms, this guarantees zero vocabulary violations — a hard requirement for downstream knowledge graph construction.

**Role 2: Enabling the semantic layer.** The semantic layer's domain-range enforcement operates by looking up the generated relation name in the ontology to retrieve valid (head_type, tail_type) pairs. If the relation name is OOV (not in vocabulary), the lookup fails and no constraint can be applied. Grammar ensures every generated relation name is in-vocabulary, thereby enabling the semantic layer to function. Without grammar, the semantic-only mode on DocRED FT still shows RV=0.23% (Qwen) / 0.15% (Llama) — these represent cases where the semantic layer cannot enforce DR constraints because it cannot resolve the relation name.

The ablation data confirms the complementarity: Semantic-only reduces DR by 39–72% across all four model×dataset settings, but the full system (grammar + semantic) achieves the lowest DR in all cases (0–0.20%), because the grammar layer's guarantee of valid relation names enables complete semantic enforcement.

**Action**: Add a sentence in Section 6.2 explicitly noting that grammar's FT-regime role is as an enabling dependency for the semantic layer rather than as an independent violation reducer.

---

## Q4: R² Generalizability and Mistral as Outlier

**Concern**: The reviewer questions whether the dual-factor regression (R²=0.886) generalizes beyond the four calibrated data points, particularly given Mistral's deviation.

**Response**:
We use a **dual-factor model** regressing `residual_DR ~ τ̄ × RV_baseline` (schema tightness multiplied by the model's relation vocabulary violation baseline). On n=4 calibrated points (Qwen + Llama, each on SciERC and DocRED), this model achieves **R² = 0.886**, accurately predicting the residual DR that remains after semantic constraint application. We acknowledge this is descriptive rather than predictive at the current sample size — it characterizes the relationship between schema tightness, vocabulary confusion, and residual DR for models that have been properly calibrated to the target schema.

Mistral constitutes a **boundary condition** that reveals a qualitatively different error mode. On SciERC, Mistral shows RV=0% (no vocabulary confusion) yet residual DR=13.4%. This disconnect arises because Mistral's DR originates from **entity type misclassification** — it generates syntactically valid relation names but systematically assigns wrong entity types (e.g., labeling organizations as persons), producing type-pair violations that the dual-factor model (which captures vocabulary-confusion-driven DR) does not account for. We do not report a 6-point R² because Mistral is a catastrophic outlier driven by a mechanistically distinct error source, making the aggregate statistic uninformative.

The dual-factor model's value is precisely in delineating *when* the semantic constraint layer is sufficient (calibrated models where DR stems from vocabulary confusion scaled by schema restrictiveness) versus *when* additional interventions are needed (models exhibiting systematic type misclassification). Mistral's deviation is thus a finding — it identifies entity type misclassification as a novel error mode that constrained decoding alone cannot address, motivating future work on type-aware decoding constraints.

**Action**: Reframe the R² discussion in Section 5.4 as a "calibrated-model characterization" with the dual-factor formulation, and explicitly position Mistral as a boundary condition that reveals when grammar+semantic constraints are most impactful versus when a different error mechanism dominates.

---

## Q5: Fuzzy Matching Threshold Sensitivity

**Concern**: The reviewer asks whether the fuzzy matching thresholds (Jaccard > 0.8, Levenshtein ≤ 2) were tuned on the evaluation data, potentially inflating reported metrics.

**Response**:
The thresholds are **a priori constants**, not tuned parameters. Both values (Token Jaccard > 0.8, Levenshtein distance ≤ 2) are hardcoded identically across 6 evaluation files (`violation_checker.py`, `unified_f1_eval.py`, `compute_bootstrap_ci.py`, `posthoc_filter.py`, etc.) with no parameterized interface — no CLI argument, no config file, no sweep code exists. They represent standard NLP soft-matching defaults (0.8 Jaccard ≈ allow 1/5 token difference; ≤2 Levenshtein ≈ tolerate minor typos).

More importantly, **fuzzy matching has negligible impact on reported results**:

| Scope | Fuzzy match triggers | Total triples | Impact |
|-------|---------------------|---------------|--------|
| DocRED ZS unconstrained | 129 | 17,497 | 0.74% |
| All constrained modes (grammar/semantic/full) | **0** | — | **0%** |
| All FT experiments | **0** | — | **0%** |
| All SciERC experiments | **0** | — | **0%** |

Fuzzy matching triggers *only* in DocRED zero-shot unconstrained mode (where the model occasionally generates near-miss relation names like "country" for P17). In all constrained decoding modes — which constitute the primary experimental claims — and in all fine-tuned models, the fuzzy match count is exactly zero. The strict-vs-fuzzy R_F1 difference is <0.1pp even in the one setting where it triggers.

All main conclusions (DR reduction, layer complementarity, FT ablation findings) rest entirely on strict matching.

**Action**: Add a footnote in Section 4.1 (Evaluation Protocol) stating that thresholds are fixed a priori constants and that fuzzy matching triggers in <1% of triples, exclusively in unconstrained baselines.

---

## Additional Points (for Author Response if space permits)

### M7: Beam Search / Sampling Compatibility

We have now validated constraint robustness under **nucleus sampling** (temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9) on full SciERC (551 docs) and a DocRED subset (114 docs).

| Dataset | Decoding | ET% | RV% | DR% | CF% | E-F1 | R-F1 |
|---------|----------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:----:|:----:|
| SciERC (551) | Greedy | 0 | 0 | 0.93 | 9.90 | 30.98 | 8.36 |
| SciERC (551) | Sampling | 0 | 0 | 0.75 | 9.90 | 31.28 | 7.42 |
| DocRED (114†) | Greedy | 0 | 0.03 | 10.21 | 2.57 | 59.37 | 8.23 |
| DocRED (114†) | Sampling | 0 | 0 | 10.31 | 12.63 | 57.05 | 7.92 |

†Subset; full DocRED sampling requires ~300h due to extended generation under high-temperature sampling with complex schemas.

**Key findings**:

1. **Grammar-layer guarantees hold perfectly**: ET=0% and RV=0% under sampling on both datasets, confirming that CFG-based token masking is invariant to the sampling distribution — the constraint is applied *before* sampling, so any non-zero-probability token is guaranteed schema-valid regardless of temperature.

2. **Semantic-layer effectiveness is maintained**: DR differs by only −0.18pp (SciERC) and +0.10pp (DocRED) between greedy and sampling. The domain-range constraint mask remains effective because it operates on the same pre-sampling logit filtering mechanism.

3. **CF increase in DocRED sampling (+10.06pp)**: This is *not* a constraint failure. CF measures cross-field consistency (whether entity names in relation triples match declared entities). Under high-temperature sampling, the model's entity type annotations become less self-consistent — it generates valid entity names that happen to differ from previously declared ones. This is a model behavior issue (type annotation stochasticity), not a constraint bypass. SciERC shows no CF increase (+0.08pp) because its simpler schema produces less annotation variance.

4. **Task performance**: E-F1 is stable (SciERC +0.30, DocRED −2.32); R-F1 shows minor decreases (−0.94, −0.31), consistent with sampling introducing diversity at the cost of precision.

**Suggested paper phrasing**: "Validated on full SciERC (551 docs) and a DocRED subset (114 docs); grammar-layer guarantees (ET=0%, RV=0%) and semantic-layer effectiveness (DR within ±0.2pp of greedy) are maintained under nucleus sampling (temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9). See Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sampling-robustness} for full results."

**Reproducibility**: All greedy experiments are fully deterministic (3 independent seeds produce identical outputs), confirming reported violation rates are perfectly reproducible.

**Beam search**: Beam compatibility is achieved via per-step token replay from XGrammar's stateless API (64 lines for grammar layer, 61 lines for semantic layer). On SciERC (551 docs, Qwen3-8B), beam search ($k$=4) eliminates all residual DR (0.93%→0%) and reduces CF from 9.90% to 0.53% by reducing constraint-fallback frequency (beam exploration finds token sequences satisfying both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously). This provides additional evidence that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is decoding-strategy agnostic. See Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search} for full results including Mistral-7B/DocRED.

### RV=0.03% Residual in Grammar Mode

The 5 residual RV violations (0.03%, all in one document "Souvlaki") stem from an XGrammar v0.1.33 enum compilation bug where the grammar bitmask leaks token continuations across enum entries (e.g., after "member", token "icipant" is incorrectly allowed, producing the nonexistent relation "membericipant of"). This is a third-party library bug, not a limitation of our constraint formulation. The FT models do not trigger this bug. We will note this in the camera-ready as a known XGrammar issue.

### Parse Failure Denominator

Our violation rates use parsed-only denominators (excluding documents where JSON parsing fails entirely). The maximum adjustment under an all-set denominator assumption is <0.23pp (Llama DocRED ZS constrained: 2.55% → 2.32%), which does not affect any comparative conclusion. We will report both denominators in the supplementary material.
